entries.title: Ask this book feature now on Kindle ereaders
entries.summary: Kindle Software Update 5.20.2 brings the AI-powered "Ask This Book" feature directly to Kindle e-readers. The post Ask this book feature now on Kindle ereaders first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon’s Kindle Software Update 5.20.2 brings the AI-powered “Ask This Book” feature directly to Kindle e-readers.

This feature acts as an interactive, built-in reading companion. It allows you to query the text, generate summaries, or ask specific questions about characters and plot points without risking outside spoilers.

Noted by users as one of the largest firmware installation files Amazon has released to date. It is around 643 MB in size.

You can access it by opening the in-book menu or by highlighting a specific passage or word within the text. It will provide a list of suggested questions, or you can type your own custom question and ask follow-ups

Michael Kozlowski is the editor-in-chief at Good e-Reader and has written about audiobooks and e-readers for the past fifteen years. Newspapers and websites such as the CBC, CNET, Engadget, Huffington Post and the New York Times have picked up his articles. He Lives in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.

entries.title: Book Piracy Is Going Automated as Publishers Fight Back
entries.summary: In March 2026, thirteen major publishers sued a website that aims to… The post Book Piracy Is Going Automated as Publishers Fight Back first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
In March 2026, thirteen major publishers sued a website that aims to gather every book in the world. The case illustrates the current state of book piracy and explains why it is so difficult to stop. The following offers a simple look at what happened, how serious the problem is, and why takedowns, site blocks, and lawsuits are increasingly handled by automation.

What Happened in the March 2026 Lawsuit

On March 6, 2026, the Association of American Publishers (AAP) filed a lawsuit against Anna’s Archive, with thirteen members joining the suit, including Penguin Random House, HarperCollins, Hachette, Simon & Schuster, Elsevier, and Wiley. The case, named Apress Media et al. v. Anna’s Archive, was filed in the federal court in Manhattan.

The plaintiffs claim willful copyright infringement. They argue that the operation runs book piracy as a commercial enterprise, using “donations” which function as memberships. The complaint includes 130 examples of works, ranging from Jonathan Franzen’s The Corrections to PowerPoint 2019 For Dummies. Maria Pallante, chief of AAP, described it as a “brazen pirate operation.” Since the individuals involved are anonymous, the lawsuit refers to them only as “Does 1-10”.

Ebook Piracy by the Numbers

So what is the current scale of book piracy? The complaint gives two remarkable figures:

  • More than 63 million books and 95 million papers, about one petabyte of data.
  • Roughly 763,000 downloads a day, based on the operation’s own 30-day average on March 3, 2026.

It’s important to have some context for these figures, since they are based on the plaintiffs’ figures and the pirate platform’s own counts, meaning they are claims, not verified totals. Furthermore, a download does not always represent a lost sale because some people would never have paid for the book.

The damage is still there. Such collections are often called shadow libraries, but the people who brought the case do not accept that term. Genuine libraries lend out books that they have purchased legally. Meanwhile, each free copy can mean a lost sale and lost royalties for the author. While digital rights management locks can hinder simple copying, a determined uploader can remove them, which is why enforcement generally begins after a leak has occurred.

How the Industry Responds: Courts, Registries, and Search

The industry uses three primary tools to combat book piracy, and each has a drawback.

Tool What it targets The catch
Lawsuit and damages The anonymous operators Payment is very unlikely
Registry and host orders Website addresses Foreign registries may ignore US orders
Search removals Google results The platform is still easy to find

The case progressed rapidly. On May 19, 2026, Judge Jed Rakoff entered default judgment because the operators had not appeared. He awarded the maximum statutory damages of $150,000 for each of the 130 works. That amounts to $19.5 million in total.

The injunction is more significant since it requires over twenty registries, registrars, and hosts — including Cloudflare — to switch off the remaining domains. This is domain blocking at the source. Yet, in August, TorrentFreak reported that the piracy platform was still accessible via .gl, .pk, and .gd addresses managed by registries outside the United States. Legal pressure on providers such as Cloudflare is forcing operators to change their setup.

Search is also one front in the battle against book piracy. By the end of 2025, Google had verified 749 million removals related to addresses on its platform, about 5 percent of all URLs reported since 2012 on copyright grounds. Nevertheless, when searching by name, the main domain still appeared first. Put simply, delisting websites from search engines removes individual book pages without hiding the main entrance.

Book Piracy News: Enforcement Goes Automated as AI Joins In

The key change is that enforcement is now largely automated. By the end of 2025, rights holders were reporting about 10 million new URLs per week for this single platform. Human teams cannot keep up with the volume. A Dutch firm, Linkbusters, files millions of automated takedown requests on behalf of publishers, so many DMCA notices are now generated automatically.

Court orders have followed the pattern of the music labels’ earlier case against the site, which named some of the same intermediaries. Checking whether blocks are working takes real effort, and rights holders and anti-piracy teams often buy proxy access to view regional versions of a pirate site as local visitors do.

The involvement of AI creates pressure. The complaint states that the operators offered high-speed access to over 140 million texts to companies in China, Russia, and other countries, some of which were developing language models. The site also encourages developers to make an “enterprise-level donation”, and a reported crypto price of $200,000 grants full access.

The complaint cites a California court as finding that Meta downloaded the collection while developing its Llama model. The plaintiffs argue that this reduces the market for licensed AI training data.

Note that these are allegations, and a default judgment was entered because the operators did not answer when called upon in court, so the claims were not tested at trial.

What It Means for Readers and Authors

Book piracy affects authors most directly. The availability of free copies reduces sales, and pirated material can also end up in AI systems without permission. If you write, publish, or read books, then a few measures can help:

  • For authors: Check with your publisher to see whether a monitoring service is already filing takedown requests on your books’ behalf. The Google report indicates that over 1,000 authors and publishers have sent notices regarding this platform.
  • For readers: Avoid pirating books; instead, buy them or borrow them from legitimate bookstores and library apps.
  • For everyone: Watch the AI licensing debate. It is likely to be the next big fight over books.

The struggle against book piracy is far from over. Although the courts have handed down substantial judgments, U.S. orders may not be enforceable in foreign registries. This gap is likely to lead to calls for stricter domain-blocking rules, particularly for site-blocking. Progress will come in small steps, with each step making it a bit harder to find pirated

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.

entries.title: Already Own a Kindle? Do You Need a XTEINK Pocket E-Reader Too?
entries.summary: Many readers already have a Kindle. It works so well for long… The post Already Own a Kindle? Do You Need a XTEINK Pocket E-Reader Too? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Many readers already have a Kindle. It works so well for long reading sessions. But a Kindle does not fit in your pocket. That’s why it often stays at home. For shorter breaks in your day, such as during a train ride, a queue at the bank, or a wait at the doctor’s office, most people end up using their phone. This is where the XTEINK X3 comes in. It is a very small E Ink reader that weighs just about 58g and is 5.1mm thin. It can attach magnetically to the back of a compatible phone. You can read on it while it stays attached, or you can remove it and use it on its own.

Two Readers, Two Different Jobs

The X3 is not designed to replace a Kindle. It is more of a companion to it, as both devices suit a different reading situation. The Kindle obviously remains the more comfortable choice for reading on a sofa. The X3 is built for the small moments in between. Because it can ride on your phone and can slip into your pocket, it is much, much easier to keep nearby. Kindle cannot simply go into a pocket, while the X3 can. This allows you to read in moments when you would otherwise scroll on your phone.

What the X3 Offers

The X3 is the smallest model in the XTEINK lineup. It has a 3.7-inch E Ink screen with a resolution of 259 PPI. Here are its key specs:

Display: 3.7-inch E Ink, 259 PPI

Size and weight: 97.6 × 63.7 × 5.1 mm, 58g

Controls: Physical page-turn buttons and shake-to-turn

Battery: 650mAh, up to 10 to 14 days at 1 to 3 hours of reading per day (according to XTEINK)

Storage: 16GB microSD card included, expandable up to 256GB

Connectivity: 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth

Touchscreen and front light: No

Pages can be turned either with the physical buttons or with a gentle shake. This allows one-handed reading, for example, when you are holding a handrail on a bus. You can also customise the screen with photos and widgets. The X3 also includes an NFC function that supports unencrypted access cards. There is no front light, so reading in dim light needs an extra light source. Thankfully, XTEINK also sells a magnetic reading light separately.

What Kindle Owners Should Know About Books

The X3 is not connected to the Kindle Store. Books bought from Amazon are just for Kindle devices and apps, so they cannot simply be moved to the X3. The X3 supports EPUB and TXT files directly. PDF and MOBI files may not be fully supported, so XTEINK recommends converting them through the official app. Here’s how you can get books onto the device:

1. Save the book or file on your phone or computer

2. Send it to the X3 through the XTEINK app over Wi-Fi, or copy it to the microSD card

3. Read directly on the back of your phone, or remove the reader and use it on its own

The X3 works with the official XTEINK app only and does not support any third-party apps.

What to Check Before Buying

There are a few key points that you should consider before you buy the X3. First of all, do check the magnetic fit. Even though the device includes two adhesive metal rings, you should first test the setup with your own phone and case. You also need to consider the screen size. The 3.7-inch display is smaller than a Kindle screen. Those readers who want more screen space may prefer a larger model, but the small size is why you might want to buy it. Carrying it in your pocket is the whole point.

X3, X4 Classic or X4 Pro?

XTEINK currently offers three models. The X3 is the smallest and lightest at about 58g. The X4 Classic has a larger 4.3-inch screen with buttons on both sides and weighs about 68g. The X4 Pro keeps the 4.3-inch screen but adds a touchscreen and an adjustable warm and cool front light. It weighs about 72g. The X4 Pro was also named one of TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026.

The X4 Classic also supports USB-C charging through its magnetic charging adapter and can be placed on a desk with the XTEINK Base Stand, currently included as a gift.

As a simple guide, go for:

X3, if you want the smallest and lightest option

X4 Classic, if you want more reading space with button controls

X4 Pro, if you often read in low-light conditions or want a touchscreen

XTEINK’s Halloween promotion runs from October 21 to 31, 2026, featuring special offers on the X4 Classic and X3. The X3 will be 13% off from October 24 to 31, with a promotional price of approximately $69 in the US. Halloween deals will also be available on Amazon, although discounts may vary by platform.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.

entries.title: Should You Buy a Kindle If You Already Own a Tablet? A Guide for Avid E-Readers
entries.summary: If you already own a tablet, buying a Kindle might seem unnecessary.… The post Should You Buy a Kindle If You Already Own a Tablet? A Guide for Avid E-Readers first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
If you already own a tablet, buying a Kindle might seem unnecessary. After all, your tablet can display ebooks, open digital libraries, and let you read articles without requiring another device. However, avid readers may discover that a dedicated e-reader offers advantages that a multipurpose tablet cannot fully replicate.

The decision depends on how often you read, how comfortable you feel reading on a screen, and whether you want a device dedicated to books. For people who spend hours reading novels, nonfiction, or long-form articles, a Kindle can be a worthwhile addition rather than a replacement for an existing tablet.

Just as people choose different devices for different digital activities, readers may prefer a Kindle for books and a tablet for browsing, productivity, and entertainment. Someone who occasionally explores digital platforms such as Jiliph on GameZone, for example, may appreciate keeping entertainment applications on a tablet while using a Kindle to maintain a more focused reading routine.

Why Buy a Kindle When You Already Have a Tablet?

The biggest reason to consider a Kindle is that it is designed around reading. Although tablets offer more features, those additional capabilities do not necessarily improve the experience of reading a 400-page novel.

A Kindle typically uses an E Ink display that resembles printed paper. Most models also include adjustable front lighting, while selected versions offer additional lighting features. This design makes dedicated e-readers particularly appealing to people who read for extended periods.

A tablet remains useful for many other activities, including video streaming, web browsing, note-taking, and gaming. However, its LCD or OLED screen, notifications, and app switching can make it easier to lose concentration.

If reading is a major part of your daily routine, separating books from other digital activities may be a practical investment.

1. A More Comfortable Experience for Long Reading Sessions

Screen comfort is one of the strongest reasons avid readers consider buying a Kindle.

E Ink displays reflect ambient light rather than producing the same continuously illuminated appearance as conventional tablet screens. This can make text feel more like a printed page, especially when reading outdoors or in bright surroundings.

A Kindle can also reduce the temptation to switch between applications. When your device is primarily intended for books, it is easier to settle into a reading session without checking messages or opening unrelated apps.

However, a Kindle does not automatically eliminate eye strain. Poor lighting, small fonts, long uninterrupted sessions, and dry eyes can affect comfort on any device. Tablets can also be adjusted with larger text, lower brightness, and appropriate display settings.

Consider a Kindle if: you regularly read for 30 minutes or longer and find your tablet distracting or uncomfortable.

2. Longer Battery Life for Everyday Reading

Battery life is another practical advantage of dedicated e-readers.

Kindle models generally last much longer between charges than tablets under typical reading conditions. E Ink displays use relatively little power to maintain a static page, although wireless connectivity, lighting, and other features influence actual battery performance.

For avid readers, this means fewer charging interruptions during commutes, vacations, or weekend reading sessions.

A tablet consumes more power because it supports a brighter display, a more powerful processor, and background applications. Reading alone may not drain it quickly, but switching between books, videos, browsers, and games can increase battery consumption.

If you already carry a tablet and a phone, a Kindle’s extended battery life can make it a convenient companion for travel.

3. Fewer Distractions and Better Reading Habits

Having a dedicated reading device can help establish a consistent reading routine.

On a tablet, a book may compete with social media, notifications, streaming services, and entertainment applications. Even a quick notification check can turn a planned reading session into an extended browsing session.

A Kindle provides a simpler environment. Depending on the model and configuration, you can focus on your library, adjust your reading settings, and continue where you stopped.

This separation can be useful if you want to read before bed, during lunch breaks, or while commuting. Meanwhile, your tablet can remain available for other activities, including digital entertainment such as Jiliph on GameZone.

The benefit is not that entertainment is inherently incompatible with reading. Rather, using separate devices can make it easier to choose the activity you intended to do.

4. When Your Tablet Is Already Enough

Despite its advantages, a Kindle is not essential for every tablet owner.

If you read only occasionally, your current device may already provide everything you need. A tablet is especially useful for content that depends on color, interactive elements, or complex page layouts.

Students who frequently annotate PDFs, researchers who switch between documents, and readers who enjoy illustrated magazines may prefer a tablet’s larger, more versatile display.

A tablet also makes it easier to use multiple reading applications without being limited to a particular ecosystem. Kindle devices support selected formats and services, but compatibility varies, so check your ebook library before purchasing one.

If your tablet feels comfortable, offers sufficient battery life, and does not distract you, buying another device may provide only a modest improvement.

Kindle vs. Tablet: Which Offers More Value?

Consideration Kindle Existing tablet
Long reading sessions E Ink suits text-heavy reading Depends on display and personal comfort
Battery life Generally longer Usually shorter
Distractions Fewer applications on most models More notifications and app options
Color content Limited on many models Better for illustrated material
Productivity Limited compared with tablets Supports multiple work applications
Best investment Frequent, dedicated reading Occasional or mixed-use reading

5. How to Decide Before Spending Money

Before purchasing a Kindle, evaluate your actual reading habits instead of buying one simply because it is popular among book lovers.

Ask yourself three questions:

  • How frequently do I read? Daily readers are more likely to benefit than people who finish a book every few months.
  • What frustrates me about my tablet? Eye comfort, battery life, weight, and distractions are meaningful reasons to consider a dedicated e-reader.
  • What content do I read? Novels and text-heavy nonfiction suit Kindle devices particularly well, while colorful PDFs and illustrated publications may be better on tablets.

You should also compare the Kindle’s price with your budget and existing ebook subscriptions. If purchasing a dedicated e-reader would create financial pressure, optimizing your current tablet is a reasonable alternative.

The same practical approach applies to digital entertainment choices. Whether you use a tablet for reading or explore services such as Jiliph on GameZone, the best setup is the one that fits your needs without encouraging unnecessary spending.

Final Verdict: Is a Kindle Worth Buying?

Yes, a Kindle can be worth buying even if you already own a tablet, particularly if you are an avid reader who values extended reading comfort, long battery life, portability, and fewer distractions.

However, if you read occasionally, depend on colorful content, or already enjoy reading on your tablet, you may not need a second device.

The smartest decision is to identify what your tablet fails to provide. If it regularly interrupts your reading routine or makes long sessions less enjoyable, a Kindle could be a valuable upgrade. If it already meets your needs, keep using it and invest in more books instead.

Ultimately, a Kindle is not necessary for every reader. It is most valuable when its specialized design solves a problem you experience regularly.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.

entries.title: Kindle for Android now supports handwriting
entries.summary: Amazon has recently transformed its Kindle Android app by rolling out native handwritten ebook notes, mirroring the flagship note-taking experience found on the Kindle Scribe. The post Kindle for Android now supports handwriting first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon added handwriting and stylus support to the Kindle Android app, allowing you to write handwritten notes, sticky notes, and active canvas notes directly on supported Android phones and tablets. You can write with a stylus on select Android devices such as Galaxy Tab and Onyx Boox products.

The app update also makes text in the book automatically flow around your handwritten notes, similar to the Kindle Scribe experience. You can choose different pen styles, sizes, and colors, which is useful for people who love using the Kindle app to read e-books, comics, and manga. The rollout appears to be exclusive to Android tablets and phones, as the feature has yet to find its way to Apple devices such as the iPad or iPhone.

Early user feedback has praised the feature as a massive upgrade for productivity, allowing readers to seamlessly review, annotate, and color-code text without being chained to physical paper or dedicated e-ink devices. By expanding on recent updates that introduced text underlining and outlines, Amazon has closed a frustrating gap between its mobile app and hardware readers. While Apple iPadOS users are still waiting for their version of the feature, Android users now have access to a versatile, centralized hub where typed text highlights and fluid handwriting live side by side.

Michael Kozlowski is the editor-in-chief at Good e-Reader and has written about audiobooks and e-readers for the past fifteen years. Newspapers and websites such as the CBC, CNET, Engadget, Huffington Post and the New York Times have picked up his articles. He Lives in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.

entries.title: Kindle Software update fixes Kindle Clip bugs
entries.summary: An upcoming Kindle software update fixes Bluetooth remotes, extends battery life, and includes the new Kindle+ rebrand. The post Kindle Software update fixes Kindle Clip bugs first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon is slowly rolling out a new software update for several current-generation e-readers and Scribe e-notebooks, as well as some older models. The 5.20.1.0.2 firmware fixes the Kindle Clip and other Bluetooth page-turners that don’t count page turns as user activity, so the screen would often time out and switch to the lock screen. After the update, page turns from the remote are now recognized as activity. The Kindle stays awake while you’re reading and only goes to sleep after the configured period of inactivity.

The update also switches the branding on the e-readers and e-notebooks from Kindle Unlimited to Kindle+. Amazon switched the branding last week because Kindle Unlimited suggested an unlimited number of books, while the service offers manga, magazines, audiobooks, and other digital content. The biggest change in the rebrand is a major expansion of the audiobook library, including both human-narrated titles and AI-generated narration through Amazon’s Virtual Voice program.

Social media also claims the update extends battery life by a moderate amount, giving more reading and listening time on the Kindle.

Amazon has not posted the change log yet on its website, but many Kindle users all over the world are already receiving it.
